entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen17675" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17676" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17677" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17677" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17676" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17678" type="x-p"/> Elihu accuses Job of impious speeches, <reference osisRef="Job.35.1-Job.35.4">Job 35:1-4</reference>. No man can affect God by his iniquity, nor profit him by his righteousness, <reference osisRef="Job.35.5-Job.35.8">Job 35:5-8</reference>. Many are afflicted and oppressed, but few cry to God for help; and, for want of faith, they continue in affliction, <reference osisRef="Job.35.9-Job.35.16">Job 35:9-16</reference>.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17679" type="x-p"/> My righteousness is more than God's? - This would indeed be a blasphemous saying; but Job never said so, neither directly nor constructively: it would be much better to translate the words צדקי מאל tsidki meel, I am righteous Before God. And Job's meaning most certainly was, "Whatever I am in your sight, I know that in the sight of God I am a righteous man;" and he had a right to assume this character, because God himself had given it to him.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17680" type="x-p"/> What advantage will it be unto thee? - As if he had said to God, "My righteousness cannot profit thee, nor do I find that it is of any benefit to myself." Or perhaps Elihu makes here a general assertion, which he afterwards endeavors to exemplify: Thou hast been reasoning how it may profit thee, and thou hast said, "What profit shall I have in righteousness more than in sin?"

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17682" type="x-p"/> Look unto the heavens - These heavens, and their host, God has created: the bare sight of them is sufficient to show thee that God is infinitely beyond thee in wisdom and excellence. <div eID="gen17682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17683" type="x-p"/> Behold the clouds - שחקים shechakim, the ethers, (Vulgate, aethera), from שחק shachak, to contend, fight together: the agitated or conflicting air and light; the strong agitation of these producing both light and heat. Look upon these, consider them deeply, and see and acknowledge the perfections of the Maker.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17685" type="x-p"/> Thy wickedness may hurt - It is better to translate this literally: <div eID="gen17685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17686" type="x-p"/> To a man like thyself is thy wickedness: <div eID="gen17686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17687" type="x-p"/> And to the son of man, thy righteousness: <div eID="gen17687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17688" type="x-p"/> That is: - <div eID="gen17688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17689" type="x-p"/> Thou mayest injure thyself and others by thy wickedness, <div eID="gen17689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17690" type="x-p"/> And thou mayest benefit both by thy righteousness; <div eID="gen17690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17691" type="x-p"/> But God thou canst neither hurt nor profit.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17692" type="x-p"/> By reason of the multitude - Or rather, "From among the multitude" the oppressed clamor, יזעיקו yaziku: they shout, ישועו yeshavveu, because of the mighty. The wicked rich oppress the wicked poor; these cry aloud because of their oppressors; but they have no relief, because they call not upon God.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17693" type="x-p"/> Where is God my Maker - They have no just apprehension of his being; they do not consider themselves his creatures, or that he who created them still preserves them, and would make them happy if they would pray unto him. <div eID="gen17693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17694" type="x-p"/> Who giveth songs in the night - This is variously translated. "Before whom the high angels give praise in the night." - Chaldee. "Who sets the night-watches." - Septuagint. "Gives meditations in the night." - Syriac and Arabic. "And that shyneth upon us that we might prayse him in the night." - Coverdale. <div eID="gen17694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17695" type="x-p"/> A holy soul has continual communion with God: night and day its happiness is great; and God, from whom it comes, is the continual subject of its songs of praise.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17696" type="x-p"/> Who teacheth us more than the beasts - "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib; but Israel doth not know me, my people do not consider;" <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Isa 1:3</reference>. Beasts, bards, fowls, and in many cases pond-fishes, know and seem thankful to the hand that feeds them; while man, made much more noble than they, gifted with the greatest powers, privileged with the most important benefits, considers not the Lord, nor discerns the operation of his hand. Quadrupeds, reptiles, and fowls, have more gratitude to their masters than man has to his God.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17700" type="x-p"/> Thou sayest thou shalt not see Him - Several MSS. have "Thou shalt not see me," and the Septuagint, and one other, "Thou shalt not see us," but without the points, תשורנו, the original may be read see Him or see Us, the third person singular, or the first person plural. <div eID="gen17700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17701" type="x-p"/> Yet judgment is before him - Rest assured that God has not forgotten either to punish or to save; therefore trust in him; choose to be a monument of his mercy, rather than of his justice.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen17701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17702" type="x-p"/> But - because it is not so - Rather, "But now, because he visiteth not in his anger." This is more literal than the versions generally proposed; and the sense of the place appears to be this: Because vengeance is not speedily executed on an evil work, therefore are the hearts of the children of men set in them to do iniquity. This is, in effect, the charge which Elihu brings against Job.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen17702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17703" type="x-p"/> Therefore doth Job open his mouth in vain - God will execute vengeance when it may best serve the ends of his justice, providence, and mercy. The delay of judgment is not proof that it shall not be executed; nor is the deferring of mercy any proof that God has forgotten to be gracious. <div eID="gen17703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17704" type="x-p"/> He multiplieth words without knowledge - However this may apply to Job, it most certainly applies very strongly and generally to the words, not only of Job's three friends, but to those also of Elihu himself. The contest is frequently a strife of words.  <chapter eID="Job.35"/> <div eID="gen17704" type="x-p"/>
